Female Atlantic lizardfish reach a maximum total length of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters], a size rarely exceeded in field surveys conducted throughout their Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic range. This ultimate length is attained only after several years of steady somatic growth, during which individuals allocate resources primarily to increasing body size before shifting investment toward gonadal development. The onset of reproductive capability is marked by the total length at puberty for females, which has been recorded at 16.6 centimeters [Lp = 16.6 centimeters]. Males tend to mature at a slightly smaller size, although the difference is not substantial. These length-based thresholds are critical for fisheries management, as they help define the minimum capture size that allows a sufficient proportion of the population to reproduce before being harvested. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this pattern of delayed maturation until a relatively large body size is common among lizardfishes, likely reflecting the advantages of size-related fecundity gains in a batch-spawning life history.

Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from fertilised ova that are remarkably small, with a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.00038 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00038 grams]. This minuscule initial mass is consistent with the egg diameter of around 0.9 millimeters observed in the closely related Saurida undosquamis, from which the birth weight estimate was derived through geometric approximation. At this stage, the non-feeding larva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves, absorbing nutrients from the yolk sac as it develops its mouth and digestive system. The endotrophic period lasts only a few days before the yolk is fully depleted, at which point the exotrophic transition occurs and the larva must commence active feeding on planktonic prey. Such a small birth mass places the species at the lower end of the size spectrum for marine teleosts, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritizes high fecundity over large offspring size. This early vulnerability is offset by the production of numerous eggs during each spawning event.

Under local thermal conditions averaging 19.8 °C [T = 19.8 °C], the lifespan of Synodus saurus reaches a maximum of 4015 days [am = 4015 days]. This longevity is comparatively modest among benthic marine fishes of similar body size, though it is consistent with the pace of life documented for other members of the family Synodontidae. Mortality in this species is likely driven by predation from larger piscivores, including groupers and larger mackerels, rather than by senescence alone. Seasonal water temperature fluctuations may modulate the rate of physiological aging, with warmer conditions potentially accelerating metabolic wear and tear. Field mark-recapture studies have confirmed that few individuals survive beyond the age of eight years, making the eleven-year maximum an upper bound reached only under particularly favorable circumstances. The relatively short lifespan is offset by an early onset of reproductive activity and a high annual reproductive output.

At a total length of 31 centimeters, which corresponds to a fully mature adult, females produce two spawning events per year [F_R_i = two spawning events per year], each containing approximately 58599 eggs per event [N_R_i = approximately 58599 eggs per event], measured under controlled laboratory conditions at 19.8 °C [T = 19.8 °C]. This high fecundity is characteristic of batch-spawning teleosts that release pelagic eggs into the water column, where survival to hatching is stochastic and density-dependent. The two annual spawning peaks coincide with periods of elevated primary productivity, ensuring that larvae encounter adequate food availability during their first exogenous feeding. The reproductive output per female per year is substantial, contributing to the species' ability to maintain stable populations despite high early-life mortality. Such a strategy, prioritizing high fecundity over parental investment, is typical of many lizardfishes inhabiting temperate and subtropical shelves.

The ultimate wet weight for females has been estimated at 553 grams [Wwi = 553 grams], a value derived from a length-weight relationship specific to this species. This asymptotic mass is attained only after growth decelerates markedly following the onset of sexual maturation, reflecting the energetic trade-off between continued somatic expansion and reproductive allocation. Females of this size are capable of producing the large clutches described above, and their body condition directly influences egg quality and larval viability. Comparisons with related species show that the length-weight scaling exponent is consistent with the general pattern for demersal fishes with a fusiform body shape. The species' maximum recorded body mass in adults places it among the mid-sized benthic predators in its community, occupying a trophic niche that bridges small forage fish and larger piscivorous teleosts. As with many marine fishes, the relationship between length and mass becomes increasingly variable at larger sizes due to differences in recent feeding history and reproductive state.
